title: Semiconductor nanofilms as thermal phonon polarizers: competing effects of scattering selection rules and boundary mode conversion
abstract: Phonon scattering selection rules are known to control heat flow through bulk solids. Here we show that these selection rules also modulate heat flow through nanoscale semiconductor films, although through a previously-unexplored mechanism. Using first-principles calculations, we expose a competition between these selection rules and phonon mode conversion at boundaries of nanoscale films, that drives mode-polarized heat currents at cryogenic temperatures ($\le$ 100 K). This polarizing effect is stronger in materials like indium phosphide, where selection rules based on large velocity differences between phonon branches amplifies the longitudinal acoustic (LA) phonon contribution to thermal conductivity by restricting their intrinsic scattering events, while boundary mode conversion in nanoscale films suppresses it by depopulating the LA phonons. The resulting transverse-polarized non-equilibrium phonons will enable symmetry-selective engineering of phonon coupling to electrons, strains and defects in nanoscale films, that is difficult to achieve in bulk solids.
summary: This work analyzes how phonon scattering rules interact with boundary reflections in semiconductor nanofilms, leading to unique mode-polarized heat currents at low temperatures. By simulating these competing effects using first-principles methods, the authors show that this polarization allows for unprecedented control over phonon coupling compared to bulk materials.
main_problem: The paper investigates how phonon scattering selection rules compete with boundary mode conversion effects to modulate heat flow in nanoscale semiconductor films.
main_result: This competition leads to phonon mode-polarized heat currents, enabling symmetry-selective engineering of phonon coupling that is difficult to achieve in bulk solids.
method: The study uses first-principles calculations solving the steady-state Peierls-Boltzmann equation (SSPBE) via a variance-reduced Monte Carlo approach.
model_or_system: The physical system involves semiconductor nanofilms, specifically InP and BP, where heat transport is governed by phonon scattering mechanisms at cryogenic temperatures. The model explicitly accounts for intrinsic selection rules and extrinsic boundary reflections/mode conversions.
key_observables: Thermal conductivity ($\kappa$), phonon mode-polarized heat currents, LA and TA phonon contributions.
important_parameters: Cryogenic temperatures ($\le 100$ K), film thickness ($d$), material type (InP vs BP).
main_assumptions: The Relaxation Time Approximation (RTA) is used; boundary conditions model conserving incoming/outgoing heat fluxes normal to adiabatic boundaries.
figures_summary: Figures show the dependence of thermal conductivity ($\kappa'$) on film thickness ($d$), comparing scenarios with and without mode conversion, and illustrate spectral contributions to $\kappa$ normalized by bulk values.
paper_structure: The paper builds from established knowledge of phonon selection rules in bulk solids to model the competition between these rules and boundary mode conversion effects in thin films, culminating in predictions for engineered thermal properties.
why_interesting: While focused on phonons (lattice vibrations), the concept of non-equilibrium energy transport and symmetry-selective coupling is relevant to understanding heat dissipation in quantum devices or open quantum systems where boundaries play a crucial role.

The phonon dispersions along other high-symmetry directions for these materials are shown in Supplementary Figs. S1(a)-(b). LA and TA phonon dispersions are farther apart in InP than in BP, thus activat- ing the AAA # 2 selection rule in InP [2].

FIG. 2. Effect of mode conversion on the κ of BP and InP thin films at 100 K. (a) Thin film κ of BP and InP vs. thickness (d) normalized by the corresponding bulk values (κb) at 100 K. The inset shows the simulation geometry, and the incidence (θin) and the reflection (θout) angles for a phonon undergoing mode conversion at the thin film boundary. For specular reflection without mode conversion, the κ’s of thin films are equal to κb, independent of d [20]. When mode conversion is allowed, the predicted κ’s for specular reflections decrease faster with d in InP than in BP. FIG. 3. The normalized material factor Dλvλ of the mode conversion probabilities in InP (a) and BP (b). The x-axis is truncated at the maximum ν of the TA2 branch, beyond which mode conversion does not occur for the LA phonons [Fig. 2 (b)], since DTA1 λ = DTA2 λ = 0. In both materials, Dλvλ is much larger for the TA phonons than for the LA phonons, with the contrast being greater for InP than BP, due to the large velocity differences of the phonon polarizations in the former.

FIG. 4. Thickness-dependent κ of InP films at different cryo- genic temperatures scaled by κb. When phonons undergo specular reflections with mode conversion, κ/κb saturates at larger d as T is lowered, due to the longer phonon MFPs at lower T. For diffuse reflections, mode conversion has no effect on κ (d) /κb.
